publications.title: A Multimodal Approach for Skin Lesion Diagnosis
publications.subtitle: IEEE Xplore
publications.description: Inspection by dermatologists remains the standard for skin cancer diagnosis, but it can be subjective and prone to error. We explore the potential of machine learning for dermoscopic image classification using 10,000 pigmented skin lesions. Although convolutional neural networks are powerful tools for skin lesion classification by themselves, by incorporating patient-specific textual data, we aim to improve the accuracy and accessibility of diagnosis. We propose multiple multimodal models: transfer learning and multimodal transformers. These multimodal approaches aim to utilise both dermoscopic images and corresponding patient-specific data, such as lesion location and patient demographics. Our multimodal model with the best overall evaluation is the multimodal transformer model which combines a vision transformer and a text transformer. It achieved an accuracy of 93.21% and an AUROC of 0.9860.

projects.title: ARRAI
projects.description: ARRAI is an AI-powered inspection system designed to pair directly with wearable devices like Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses to modernize heavy machinery inspections. Instead of carrying clipboards or manually documenting findings, inspectors can simply record components in the field using the glasses, capturing first-person video and images hands-free. That media is automatically ingested into ARRAI’s cloud pipeline, where computer vision and audio analysis models detect component-level defects and anomalies. A fine-tuned language model then converts those structured detections into clear, standardized inspection issues and generates a CAT-style report aligned with industry documentation standards. By combining wearable capture, automated analysis, and structured report generation, ARRAI transforms raw field footage into professional inspection documentation in near real time, reducing manual effort while improving accuracy and consistency.

projects.title: Lexora
projects.description: I built and deployed an end-to-end cloud AI system that transforms raw contract PDFs into structured, clause-level risk insights and negotiation guidance. The platform uses a dual-model architecture that combines deterministic machine learning with grounded LLM reasoning to avoid hallucination-prone, LLM-only workflows. At its core is ClauseRiskNet, a custom clause classification and risk-scoring model (0–100) with confidence estimates, supported by multi-stage inference fallbacks (ONNX → sklearn → heuristic rules) to ensure reliability and reproducibility. The system implements a full document pipeline, including PDF extraction, clause segmentation, ML inference, risk aggregation, and persistent storage for auditability. A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) layer powers negotiation playbooks and redline suggestions using clause-scoped TF-IDF retrieval and schema-validated LLM outputs. The production frontend was built with Next.js and TypeScript, featuring synchronized PDF viewing and interactive clause exploration, while the backend runs as a Dockerized FastAPI service with PostgreSQL on cloud infrastructure. The system was designed with a strong emphasis on explainability, determinism, and auditability over black-box summarization.

projects.title: Seismic Detection Across the Solar System
projects.description: • Developed a multi-modal seismic detection system integrating Support Vector Regression (SVR) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to analyze planetary seismic data• Implemented SVR models to handle nonlinear relationships, outliers, and high-dimensional feature spaces for refined seismic event predictions• Built and trained CNN architectures using 1D time-series convolutions and 2D spectrogram inputs to extract seismic features while mitigating noise• Optimized model performance using MaxPooling and Dropout layers to reduce overfitting while preserving essential seismic signal characteristics• Evaluated and compared trigger algorithms (Z-detector, STA/LTA, and others), identifying the Z-detector as the most effective for lunar seismic profiles• Improved detection accuracy by tuning off-trigger thresholds to enhance waveform edge identification without increasing false positives• Adapted lunar-trained detectors to Martian seismic data by adjusting window sizes, bandpass filters, and trigger thresholds for cross-planet generalization• Conducted comprehensive validation through waveform visualization, characteristic function analysis, and manual review of noisy samples across planetary datasets

This past Friday, I officially wrapped up my summer as a Software Engineering Intern on Cisco's Industrial IoT team in San Jose! Over the past few months, I worked on Agentic Runbook Creator (ARC) for Cisco's AI Assistant for Troubleshooting Networks. Runbooks are step-by-step diagnostic scripts used to troubleshoot industrial networks automatically, and ARC is used to generate said runbooks dynamically using context from a customer's network. My work included connecting local SLM-based hypothesis generation with cloud LLM workflows and protecting sensitive topology and device data during the handoff between on-premises and cloud activity. I also directly developed a cloud-based digital-twin evaluator that injects IOS-XE simulated faults into the customer's obfuscated topology to test whether the generated runbooks actually work. Ultimately, we brought estimated network downtime for new faults from hours to ~25 minutes, and expanded runbook coverage beyond 13 preexisting implementations! Working on ARC gave me a much better understanding of what it takes to build AI for real systems. The output needs the right context, and the workflow has to protect customer data from the start. The whole system also needs to hold up when tested against realistic failures. Taking the project from separate components to a connected workflow taught me a lot about integration and iteration, while working on an engineering team showed me how much I can learn from asking questions and listening to feedback. I'm heading back to UIUC soon, excited to keep building on these skills and apply them in future projects. I want to thank Nikhil Mathur , my mentor, and Dhananjay Awaji , my manager, for all their guidance and support throughout the summer. I'm also grateful to Elango Ganesan , Distinguished Engineer at Cisco, for taking the time to review ARC and give us invaluable feedback that helped move the project forward. Furthermore, I would like to thank Judy Heng, Alexandra Cortes , & Robin J Gonsalves (Robbie Gonsalves) for organizing events and providing amazing intern experiences. Thank you to Pranav Butaney & Srivishnu Vusirikala , my fellow intern teammates who worked alongside me on ARC. Finally, thank you to Abhishek Prabhu , Nitish G. , Nidhi Prakash , Jasraj Sidhu , & Adam Boswell , for making this summer so fun and memorable. Working at Cisco gave me stronger confidence in my abilities and a lot of great memories! #WeAreCisco #Intern

Two years ago, I graduated from UW without a job lined up or a clear plan. All I really knew was that I wanted to build a company, and I loved automating things with AI. Instead of trying to figure everything out, I tried to trust the inputs. Work somewhere I could use AI all day, learn as fast as possible, move to SF, and surround myself with people who were where I wanted to be until the right opportunity became obvious. Fast forward two years and we just wrapped up our Y Combinator batch. Norbu Sonam and I honestly believed we would both be here. We just had no idea what the path would look like. I think that’s the point. You rarely know the path, and everyone’s looks different. You just keep believing and taking the next step until one day you look up and realize you’re a lot closer than you thought. Here we are now, with a real shot at building the company we’ve always wanted. Even though the path ahead will be much longer and harder, there’s comfort in knowing the approach is the same. All we have to do is keep trusting the next step and earn our way forward.

The code was written yesterday. Why will it take 5+ weeks to go live? For decades in software development, writing code was the known bottleneck. We all knew it. We built complex processes and planning cycles around the fact that one difficult, essential thing would take a long time to complete. We optimized around engineering. But that doesn’t make sense anymore. Coding speed is no longer the constraint. Coordination is. Yet, we are still running modern, high-velocity output through legacy, low-velocity governance. When you spend millions to accelerate engineering only to stall at the approval line, you haven’t actually sped up the organization. You've just built a bigger traffic jam at the gate. The enterprise advantage no longer belongs to who can write code the fastest. It belongs to who can clear its path. Read more from Richard Newcomb , Senior Director, FDE → https://lnkd.in/grAx_WKc

Last weekend, Terac sponsored a track at the Berkeley AI Hackathon built around a simple challenge: Can you collect your own human data and use it to make an AI system better? Congratulations to the winners, MatchVision, who made soccer more accessible for blind and low-vision fans ahead of the 2026 World Cup. They started with a vision-language model and quickly discovered something surprising: modern VLMs are actually pretty bad at understanding what matters in a soccer match. The ball is small. Important actions happen off-ball. Crowd reactions don't explain why something happened. And generic video captioning models often miss the context that makes the game understandable. So instead of accepting the model's output, they built a human feedback pipeline. Using Terac, they collected annotations describing what an announcer should actually say during key moments in a match. They also collected gaze heatmaps showing where humans naturally focus their attention during play. Those two signals became training data. One taught the model where to look. And the other taught the model what was worth saying. The result wasn't just a better soccer accessibility product. It was a great example of a broader trend we're seeing across AI. For years, progress came from bigger models and bigger datasets. Increasingly, the bottleneck is becoming access to high-quality human judgment. The teams that win won't necessarily be the ones with the biggest models. They'll be the ones that can most effectively turn human expertise into training data, evaluations, and feedback loops. Shoutout to the incredible judges from the Terac team Giovanni Borgogno , Nicolás Russo , Moritz Kamke , Germán Fernández , and Vaibhav Vasudevan ! Also, a shoutout to the runners-up, Captain Ddoski, who tackled a completely different but equally important problem: helping AI systems determine whether information is actually trustworthy before acting on it.

After being head-down for the last 6 years building Sybill and shipping to 850+ customers, I think it's time to reintroduce myself. Hi, my name is Nishit. Before Sybill, I was at Stanford doing AI research in Andrew Ng's lab. The project: detecting tuberculosis in HIV-infected patients using ML. We had this bet: if you could train models on the right data, you could catch TB in HIV patients where traditional methods were missing it. It barely worked when we were building it. Now AI for healthcare diagnostics is one of the fastest-growing fields in the world. But Stanford wasn't the start. Rewind further: Bhopal kid writing detective fiction on MS Word (one of the only kids in school with a computer), then IIT Kanpur CS, then Stanford. The entrepreneurship runs in the family. My dad spent 30 years as a government engineer, then quit to start his own business. At IIT Kanpur, starting a company seemed crazy. At Stanford, my housemates were doing it. That pushed me to try. First startup with Gorish: smart shopping carts. We had an agreement with a European retail chain, and then COVID hit and retail traffic fell off a cliff. Sybill started because Gorish was teaching linear algebra remotely. 30 students on Zoom, and after two lectures: "I have no clue when my content is resonating." Invited a TA to watch faces and alert him. Then: "There should be a way to figure this out using AI." The team came together almost by accident. Gorish from Stanford AI research, now housemate. Soumyarka, who needed a place during COVID and is now our CTO. Mehak, Gorish's sister, doing AI research at Harvard, came to California and got sucked into the vortex. We built real-time body language analysis for video calls. Educators didn't care, and healthcare was curious but still not convinced. This was during a time when most people preferred to keep their cameras off. Salespeople were different: they kept their cameras on and could easily link a dollar value to every call. The first product we launched was a Google Form. You could paste a recording link and receive a summary in return. It attracted a small group of users back in 2021, before the rise of ChatGPT. Then in November 2022, OpenAI released a new model. I fed it transcripts during Thanksgiving break and was genuinely impressed by the next steps it pulled out. Mehak coded up LLM-powered call summaries the next day. ChatGPT launched a day or two later. We already had the model plugged in. Sybill is my first company that actually worked. An AI researcher who accidentally fell into sales - that's the combo that makes it work. On to the next 5 years with this team 💙
